tagline.text: An island group off eastern Quezon, reached by boat from Real

location.label: Location
location.text: Philippine Sea east of Quezon, about 25 km from mainland Luzon (Polillo, Burdeos, Panukulan, Patnanungan, Jomalig)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱2,600–3,400 (mid-range, one day on the islands, excluding transport)

children.text: The Polillo Islands are a group of about 27 islands in the Philippine Sea east of Quezon, with five municipalities: Polillo, Burdeos, Panukulan, Patnanungan and Jomalig. You cross by boat from Ungos Port in Real and can enjoy island hopping, sandbars, waterfalls and Spanish-era walls.

The Polillo Islands are a group of about 27 islands in the Philippine Sea, east of Quezon and about 25 km from mainland Luzon. The Polillo Strait separates the islands from the mainland and forms the northern edge of Lamon Bay. The main islands are Polillo Island, Patnanungan and Jomalig, and the group is divided into five municipalities: Polillo, Burdeos, Panukulan, Patnanungan and Jomalig. Polillo Island itself is split among three of them (Polillo, Burdeos and Panukulan), and the largest municipality is Polillo (population about 31,700 in 2024). The highest point is Mount Malulod, about 351 m.

Although it is fairly close to Manila, it is still little known as a tourist destination, which suits travelers who want a quiet island atmosphere. Burdeos is good for island hopping, Panukulan for its waves, Patnanungan is known for sea turtles, and Jomalig has remote beaches, each with its own appeal. Jomalig has its own entry, so see it too if you plan to go. Jomalig charges separate entry fees, and because boats cannot reach the shore, the last 100 m or so are covered by raft, according to some guides. Patnanungan is known for sea turtles and twin sandbars, but it is the quietest island with few facilities, so prepare in advance.

The history of the islands is interesting too. Before the Spanish arrived, the island is said to have been home to a polity called Pulilu, recorded in Chinese chronicles, which traded with Chinese merchants. After Juan de Salcedo visited in 1567, Spain began to rule in 1571, and a church was reportedly completed around 1577. To guard against Moro pirate raids, a stone wall with watchtowers (castillos) at its four corners was built around the town, and traces of it remain in Poblacion, Polillo. These dates follow Wikipedia and a travel guide, however; municipal and press accounts date the church and wall differently, so the exact years cannot be settled. Polillo long served as the administrative center of the island group, and Burdeos, Panukulan, Patnanungan and Jomalig were once its barrios.

Travel is simple. Take a boat from Ungos Port in Real to Polillo Port, then see Polillo town and its beaches, or continue by jeepney and tricycle to Burdeos for island hopping. Allow about 6–8 hours in total, roughly 4–5 hours by land from Manila plus 2–3 hours by boat, so a single weekend is tight and at least one night is recommended. Boat schedules and fares change often, so always check the latest timetable.
In Poblacion, Polillo, traces of a Spanish-era stone wall and corner watchtowers remain. See them together with the area around the church, said to have been completed in 1577.
A typical circuit from Burdeos covers Anilon Island, May Butas Cave, Luli Sandbar and Puting Bato Island. The sandbar disappears at high tide, so time your trip for low tide.

Puting Bato is known for its white limestone cliffs and snorkeling spots, and Pulong Kukok for being a small island home to banded sea kraits (walo-walo). Bring your own snorkel mask.
This multi-tiered waterfall is reached by a forest trail of about
30 minutes

from the village of Tamulaya (per one guide; an older account says only about 250 m on foot from the end of the village road, so it depends on where you start, and you should check locally). The rocks are slippery after rain and the current is strong, so be careful.
There is caramel-colored Bato Beach, Sabang Beach, good for sunrise, and San Francisco Beach, quiet on weekdays. Bato Beach is said to have the remains of a Japanese-era pier.
Panukulan, on the northwest of the island, is known for its waves and mangrove kayak trails. It is safer to go with a guide.

Known dishes include grilled kibit (a squid-like seafood), adobong sahang (sea snails cooked in coconut milk), and pancit habhab served on a banana leaf. Coconut oil, daing and abaca products make good souvenirs.

items.title: 2 days 1 night
items.subtitle: Polillo town and Burdeos island hopping

children.text: Leave Manila on a bus to Real from the Legarda terminal. You need an early bus to catch a morning boat.
Board the boat to Polillo at Ungos Port in Real. Guides say to check in 2 hours before departure with a valid ID, so arrive early.
Arrive at Polillo Port, have lunch and leave your bags at your lodging.
See the Spanish walls and church in Polillo town, then take a tricycle to Bato Beach or Sabang Beach for the sunset.
On the morning of the second day, take a jeepney to Burdeos. The trip is reported to take about 45 minutes.
In Burdeos, hire a boat to visit Anilon Island, Luli Sandbar and Puting Bato. Boats are often rented for up to 10 passengers.
Return to Polillo and take an afternoon boat to Real. Be sure to check the last departure time.
Boat timetables vary by day of the week and schedules can slip, so it is safest to leave a spare day.
Travel from Manila via Real to Polillo, then see the town and beaches.
Visit Tamulaya Falls in the morning, then cross to Burdeos in the afternoon for island hopping.
Watch the sunrise and return to Real on a morning boat. Morning boats are reported to be relatively calm.
Boats between the islands run only on certain days, so to reach Jomalig or Patnanungan you need to add at least one more day.

Combined RORO bus tickets that include the boat are also said to exist, so check at the terminal.

Known operators include Starhorse RORO, Syvel and Polillo Express, and timetables vary by day of the week.
Boats are also reported from Dinahican Port in Infanta and from Atimonan, besides Real. The Infanta route is said to be a little shorter, but check sailing information locally.

items.title: On the islands and between them

children.text: The Polillo–Burdeos jeepney takes about

Around town you use tricycles, pedicabs and motorcycle taxis (habal-habal). A full-day habal-habal charter is reported at about
Boats from Polillo to Jomalig and Patnanungan run only on certain days. Jomalig has no pier, so you land by raft, and there is an entry fee.

From December to May, the amihan season, the sea is relatively calm and boat travel is reliable. From June to October, the habagat season, waves are high and the Coast Guard is reported to sometimes suspend sailings. Leave some flexibility in your schedule.

Ports are crowded during Holy Week and on summer long weekends, so arrive early. The town of Polillo is reported to come alive with the town anniversary on March 18 and the feast of its patron St. Joseph on March 19.

These figures are model-based estimates (as cited on Wikipedia): annual rainfall is given as about 1,564 mm with an average of 223 rainy days, but other climate datasets put it much higher, around 2,500–3,000 mm. The wettest and driest months also differ by source, so simply expect a rainy island. In summer, when rough seas and rain overlap, island-hopping trips are often canceled.

Lodging is concentrated in Polillo town and Burdeos. For budget travelers there are small places at ₱300–800 a night, and mid-range resorts and glamping are reported at ₱1,000–2,500. Some small lodgings run on generators and may lose power in the early hours, so ask when you book. On Jomalig, hut-style lodging and camping are reported.

There is only one ATM on the islands, a Landbank machine in Polillo town, and it is reported to run out of cash on long weekends. Withdraw plenty of cash in Manila or Real. The port has no card terminals, and GCash is reported not to work reliably. LTE reaches only the town centers of Polillo and Burdeos, and power cuts are frequent, so bring a power bank.
Check in for boats about 2 hours before departure and have your ID and cash ready. Many ticket counters accept only cash.
On your return day, morning boats are said to be relatively stable, so aim for a morning sailing.
Visits to the sandbars and Anilon Island must be timed for low tide.
In the evening, mosquitoes and small sand flies are fierce in the shade of the coconut trees. Apply repellent beforehand.
Drinking water can be scarce in places, so bring a reusable bottle.
In villages, modest dress is polite. Ask people before taking their photo.
Polillo Medicare Hospital is a basic first-level facility, so serious cases may need evacuation to the mainland. Travel insurance is recommended.
Boat timetables and fares change often, so reconfirm with the operator the day before you leave.
Go with a local guide for mangrove kayaking or surfing in Panukulan, and check the schedule of the annual Panukulan Cultural Night, which is reported to be held every year.
During the habagat season (June–October), the Coast Guard may suspend sailings for several days in a row. Leave at least one spare day before your flight home.
Wear a life jacket when island hopping, and do not set out on days with high waves.
Private resort islands and protected areas restrict entry. Access to the Minasawa bird sanctuary is reported to be restricted.
Some island roads have no streetlights outside the town centers, so avoid traveling at night.
The waterfall trail is slippery after rain and the current is strong, so avoid hiking alone.
Medical care and mobile coverage are weak, so bring medicine and emergency contacts in advance.
